# ProxyHealth AI — compliance, safety and trust constraints (research as of 2026-09-23)

Scope: consumer iOS/Android/web app; user photographs medical, immigration/legal, benefits, housing and school documents; Gemini (API) explains them, extracts deadlines/amounts, produces an action plan, routes to vetted resources.

---

## 1. App-store rules: what the app must declare and disclose

### Apple App Store Review Guidelines ([developer.apple.com/app-store/review/guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/app-store/review/guidelines/))

**1.4.1 Physical harm / medical apps (verified).** "Medical apps that could provide inaccurate data or information, or that could be used for diagnosing or treating patients may be reviewed with greater scrutiny." Apps "should remind users to check with a doctor in addition to using the app and before making medical decisions." Because ProxyHealth explains lab results, discharge papers and prescriptions, expect the medical-scrutiny track; put the "check with your clinician" reminder in the UI, not only in the policy.

**5.1.1 Data collection and storage (verified).**
- (i) Privacy policy link in App Store Connect *and* in-app; must identify data collected, all uses, confirm third parties give "the same or equal protection," and "explain its data retention/deletion policies and describe how a user can revoke consent and/or request deletion."
- (ii) Consent for any user/usage data collection "even if such data is considered to be anonymous"; purpose strings must "clearly and completely describe your use of the data."
- (iii) Data minimization: "Where possible, use the out-of-process picker or a share sheet rather than requesting full access to protected resources like Photos." → Use the camera plus PHPicker; never request full photo-library access.
- (v) "If your app doesn't include significant account-based features, let people use it without a login. If your app supports account creation, you must also offer account deletion within the app." → Ship account-less by default; if accounts exist, in-app deletion is mandatory.
- (ix) "Apps that provide services in highly regulated fields (such as banking and financial services, healthcare…) or that require sensitive user information should be submitted by a legal entity that provides the services, and not by an individual developer." → Publish under an organization (LLC/nonprofit) developer account.

**5.1.2(i) Data use and sharing — third-party AI (verified; added Nov 13 2025, [developer.apple.com/news/?id=ey6d8onl](https://developer.apple.com/news/?id=ey6d8onl)).** "You must clearly disclose where personal data will be shared with third parties, including with third-party AI, and obtain explicit permission before doing so." Sending a document image to Gemini is exactly this. A privacy-policy link is not enough; show an in-app disclosure/consent before the first upload. 5.1.2(vi) adds that data from "Camera APIs, or Photo APIs… may not be used for marketing, advertising or use-based data mining, including by third parties."

**5.1.3 Health (verified).** Health/medical data may not be used for advertising, marketing or data mining; "You must disclose the specific health data that you are collecting"; and apps "may not store personal health information in iCloud" (5.1.3(ii)) → exclude extracted medical fields from iCloud backup/sync (`isExcludedFromBackup`, no CloudKit for that store).

**Privacy nutrition labels ([App Privacy Details](https://developer.apple.com/app-store/app-privacy-details/), verified).** Relevant types: *Health* ("any other user provided health or medical data"), *Sensitive Info* (race/ethnicity, disability, religion… — note immigration status is not on Apple's list but will often be inferable), *Photos or Videos*, *Other User Content*. Key definitions: "Data that is processed only on device is not 'collected'"; and data "sent to your servers then immediately discarded after servicing the request" need not be disclosed. Third-party SDK collection counts as yours. Practical consequence: if Gemini calls are transient and you retain nothing server-side, you may be able to label "Data Not Collected" for document content—**but only on the Gemini paid tier** (free tier lets Google retain/use content; see §4), and only if no analytics SDK touches document text.

**Age ratings ([developer.apple.com/news/?id=ks775ehf](https://developer.apple.com/news/?id=ks775ehf), verified).** New 13+/16+/18+ tiers; new required questions include "Medical or wellness topics"; "you must consider how all app features, including AI assistants and chatbot functionality, impact the frequency of sensitive content." Questionnaire deadline was Jan 31 2026. Because the Gemini API terms forbid use in apps "directed towards or… likely to be accessed by individuals under the age of 18" (§4), set the minimum age to 18+ and design school-document features for parents/guardians, not students.

**Accessibility Nutrition Labels (verified, [Apple Newsroom May 2025](https://www.apple.com/newsroom/2025/05/apple-unveils-powerful-accessibility-features-coming-later-this-year/)).** Optional App Store labels for VoiceOver, Voice Control, Larger Text, Sufficient Contrast, Reduced Motion, captions; Apple publishes criteria apps must meet before claiming each.

No Apple guideline currently requires a generic "this content is AI-generated" label; the AI-specific duty is the 5.1.2(i) disclosure-and-permission for sharing personal data with third-party AI. The Feb 6 and Jun 8 2026 guideline updates did not add AI-content rules (verified from the news items).

### Google Play

**Health Content and Services policy ([answer/12261419](https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/12261419), verified).** Applies to apps that "offer health-related features or information." All such developers "must complete the Health apps declaration form on the App content page." Non-device apps must state they are not a medical device and do not "diagnose, treat, cure, or prevent any medical condition" and must "remind users to consult a healthcare professional for medical advice." Privacy policy must be on "an active, publicly accessible and non-geofenced URL (no PDFs)."

**User Data policy ([answer/10144311](https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/10144311), verified).** "Personal and sensitive user data" includes health data, camera data and PII. Requires: privacy policy in Console and in-app; *prominent in-app disclosure and affirmative consent* before collecting data users would not expect (display during normal use, not buried in a menu; no consent by backing out); accurate Data safety section consistent with the policy; secure transmission ("modern cryptography (for example, over HTTPS)"); no selling of sensitive data; and, if accounts exist, deletion both "from within your app and outside of your app (for example, by visiting your website)"—freezing does not count.

**Data safety section ([answer/10787469](https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/10787469), verified).** "Collection" = transmitting data off device, but data "only stored in memory and retained for no longer than necessary to service the specific request in real-time" is exempt. "Sharing" excludes transfers to service providers processing "on behalf of the developer." → Gemini paid tier plausibly qualifies as a service provider; the *free* tier does not (Google uses content for its own products), so free-tier use would have to be declared as sharing of health/photo/document data.

**AI-Generated Content policy ([answer/13985936](https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/13985936), verified).** Apps that generate content with AI "must contain in-app user reporting or flagging features that allow users to report or flag offensive content… without needing to exit the app," and use reports to improve moderation. Prohibited outputs include content enabling deceptive behavior—Google's explainer lists "AI-generated official documentation that enables dishonest behavior" ([answer/14094294](https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/14094294), likely). → Never let the product draft or "fill in" official forms/letters that could be passed off as agency documents. Google Play, like Apple, does not require a blanket "AI-generated" label, but the flag button is mandatory.

**Photo and Video Permissions policy ([answer/14115180](https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/14115180), verified).** Apps targeting API 33+ "may only request the READ_MEDIA_IMAGES and READ_MEDIA_VIDEO permissions if system pickers… are not sufficient." Full compliance mandatory since May 28 2025. → Use CAMERA + the Android Photo Picker; do not request broad media permissions.

### Declaration checklist (both stores)
1. Privacy policy (web URL, in-app link) covering: document images and extracted text, Gemini as processor, retention (ideally none server-side), deletion, revocation.
2. In-app "before first scan" consent screen naming Google Gemini as the third-party AI and what is sent.
3. Apple privacy label + Play Data safety form answered consistently (Health, Photos, User Content; encryption in transit; deletion mechanism).
4. Play Health apps declaration; Apple Notes for Review explaining methodology and disclaimers (2.3.1 requires new features be "described with specificity").
5. Camera purpose string; photo picker instead of library access.
6. In-app report/flag control on every AI output (Play requirement; good practice on iOS).
7. Age rating 18+ (Gemini terms); "Medical or wellness topics" answered yes.
8. Account deletion in-app (Apple) and in-app + web (Google) if accounts exist; otherwise no login.
9. Organization developer account (Apple 5.1.1(ix)).

---

## 2. HIPAA, the FTC Health Breach Notification Rule, and state health-privacy law

**HIPAA does not attach.** A consumer who downloads an app to manage her own information "is not a covered entity or a business associate"; the developer "is not creating, receiving, maintaining, or transmitting PHI on behalf of a covered entity" and so "is not subject to HIPAA" (OCR, *Health App Use Scenarios & HIPAA*, Scenario 1; primary PDF at [hhs.gov](https://www.hhs.gov/sites/default/files/ocr-health-app-developer-scenarios-2-2016.pdf) — HHS blocked automated fetch; wording confirmed via [Ropes & Gray's summary](https://www.ropesgray.com/en/insights/alerts/2016/02/health-apps-and-hipaa-ocr-publishes-new-privacy-guidance-for-health-app-developers)). The FTC's [Mobile Health App Interactive Tool](https://www.ftc.gov/business-guidance/resources/mobile-health-apps-interactive-tool) (verified) frames the test: "Are you developing, offering, or operating an app on behalf of a HIPAA covered entity…?" For ProxyHealth the answer is no—unless a clinic, health plan or legal-aid grantee contracts you to deploy it to their patients/clients; then re-analyze (BA status turns on who hires/pays you).

**FTC Health Breach Notification Rule (16 CFR Part 318) very likely applies.** The 2024 amendments (final rule May 30 2024, effective July 29 2024) made explicit that the rule "applies to health apps and connected devices" not covered by HIPAA ([FTC rule page](https://www.ftc.gov/legal-library/browse/rules/health-breach-notification-rule), verified). Definitions ([16 CFR 318.2 via Cornell LII](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/16/318.2), verified):
- *Health care services or supplies* includes "any online service such as a website, mobile application… that provides mechanisms to track diseases, health conditions, diagnoses or diagnostic testing, treatment, medications…" — an app that extracts diagnoses, medications and follow-up dates from medical documents fits.
- *Personal health record*: "an electronic record of PHR identifiable health information… that has the technical capacity to draw information from multiple sources and that is managed, shared, and controlled by or primarily for the individual." FTC's guide gives as a "multiple sources" example an app that collects user input *and* syncs with another source ([FTC compliance guide](https://www.ftc.gov/business-guidance/resources/complying-ftcs-health-breach-notification-rule-0), verified). Camera captures from several providers plus user-typed corrections plus calendar export is very likely "technical capacity to draw from multiple sources."
- *Breach of security* includes "unauthorized access, including sharing of covered information without an individual's authorization" — i.e., not only hacks. Sharing document content with an AI vendor that may use it for its own purposes, without explicit authorization, is the fact pattern the FTC penalized in GoodRx ($1.5M, first HBNR action, Feb 2023; [FTC press release](https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2023/02/ftc-enforcement-action-bar-goodrx-sharing-consumers-sensitive-health-info-advertising), verified) and Premom.
- Notice: individuals within 60 calendar days of discovery; FTC at the same time if 500+ affected; media notice for 500+ in a state.
- Practical mitigant: if *no* health record is stored anywhere the developer controls (pure on-device storage, transient inference, no server persistence), the "vendor of PHR" argument weakens but does not vanish (the app itself is the record-keeping product). Treat HBNR as applicable, keep an incident-response plan, and get counsel's opinion before launch. (Applicability conclusion = my analysis; unverified as a legal opinion.)

**FTC Act §5** applies regardless: every privacy promise ("we never store your documents") must be literally true.

**State law.** Washington's My Health My Data Act (effective Mar 31 2024) covers "consumer health data" held by non-HIPAA businesses, requires consent to collect and share, and carries a private right of action ([WA AG](https://www.atg.wa.gov/protecting-washingtonians-personal-health-data-and-privacy), likely). California's CCPA/CPRA defines "sensitive personal information" to include "citizenship or immigration status" and health data (Civ. Code §1798.140(ae); [leginfo](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1798.140.), likely) — an immigration-document app processes SPI by design; offer "limit use of my sensitive personal information" and honor purpose limitation.

**FDA.** Software "intended to transfer, store, convert formats, or display" medical records/lab results is excluded from the device definition by FD&C Act §520(o)(1), *unless* it "interpret[s] or analyze[s] clinical laboratory test or other device data" ([FDA guidance](https://www.fda.gov/media/132527/download), likely). Explaining what a document *says* is display/plain-language; telling the user what their lab value *means for them* edges toward interpretation. Keep outputs at "this document reports X; ask your clinician what it means for you," and note FDA opened a comment period (through Aug 13 2026) on patient-safety impacts of excluded software.

**Trust-driven best practices (independent of legal minimums).**
- Data minimization: OCR/redact on device where feasible; strip A-numbers, SSNs, DOBs, receipt numbers, account numbers before the LLM call, or send only the text needed for the question.
- No server persistence of images or extracted fields; if any cloud state is needed, make it opt-in, encrypted, and deletable in one tap.
- Encryption at rest: iOS Data Protection (`NSFileProtectionComplete`), Android Keystore-backed encryption (EncryptedFile/Jetpack Security), exclude from cloud backups.
- No advertising/analytics SDKs with access to document content (Apple 5.1.2(vi)/5.1.3; Play "no selling").
- Immigrant-specific threat model: ICE has purchased commercial app-derived location and identity data from brokers ([EPIC](https://epic.org/documents/how-data-brokers-harm-immigrants/), likely). Server-side stores are also reachable by subpoena. Design so there is nothing to hand over.
- Plain-language privacy notice in every supported language, with the "what is sent to Google" sentence first.

## 3. Unauthorized practice of law and medical-disclaimer norms

**Who may give immigration legal advice.** USCIS: "Only an attorney or an accredited representative working for a Department of Justice recognized organization can give you legal advice and represent you in your immigration case"; "A notario público is not authorized to provide you with any legal services related to immigration" ([USCIS Common Scams](https://www.uscis.gov/scams-fraud-and-misconduct/avoid-scams/common-scams), verified). Non-attorneys "may be able to give you limited help filling out USCIS forms" and "can only charge you a nominal fee" ([USCIS Legal Services](https://www.uscis.gov/scams-fraud-and-misconduct/avoid-scams/legal-services), verified). FTC: "Only an immigration attorney or someone authorized by the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) can give you immigration advice"; others may help only with clerical tasks like typing or translating ([FTC consumer article](https://consumer.ftc.gov/articles/how-avoid-immigration-scams-and-get-real-help), verified). ILRC: consultants/notarios "cannot provide legal advice or services" ([ILRC fraud tip sheet](https://www.ilrc.org/sites/default/files/resources/avoiding_fraud_may_2021.pdf), verified).

**DOJ Recognition & Accreditation.** Partial accreditation = practice before USCIS only; full accreditation = also before immigration courts and the BIA ([EOIR R&A FAQ](https://www.justice.gov/eoir/recognition-and-accreditation-program-frequently-asked-questions), verified). Rosters: [Recognized Organizations & Accredited Representatives](https://www.justice.gov/eoir/recognition-accreditation-roster-reports); free/low-cost counsel: [EOIR List of Pro Bono Legal Service Providers](https://www.justice.gov/eoir/list-pro-bono-legal-service-providers). Complaints: DisciplinaryCounsel@uscis.dhs.gov (DHS), EOIR.Attorney.Discipline@usdoj.gov, fraud line 1-877-388-3840. → The vetted-resource DB should be built from these rosters + state bar lookups and refreshed regularly (accreditation lasts up to 3 years).

**How reputable tools word it (all verified from the live pages).**
- immi.org (Pro Bono Net/ILRC): "This Site provides information, not legal advice." "You do not become PBN's client merely by using this Site." Staff "cannot: Give you advice, opinions, or recommendations about your rights or your case." "For legal advice about your case, you should see a lawyer or a BIA accredited representative." "We do not warrant or guarantee that the information… is accurate or up-to-date." ([Terms](https://www.immi.org/en/info/Terms))
- LawHelp.org: "LawHelp.org provides general information only. This is not legal advice. You can only obtain legal advice from a lawyer." "The listing of an organization on this website does not constitute endorsement of that group." ([Disclaimer](https://www.lawhelp.org/disclaimer))
- Upsolve: "Upsolve is not a law firm or an attorney, may not perform services performed by an attorney, and its forms or templates are not a substitute for the advice or services of an attorney." "No attorney-client relationship or privilege is created with Upsolve." Users affirm "I am representing myself in this legal matter." ([Terms](https://upsolve.org/terms-of-service/))

**The line is enforced.** In *Upsolve, Inc. v. James* (2d Cir. Sept 9 2025) the court held New York's UPL statutes are content-neutral and may be applied to trained nonlawyers giving individualized advice on a check-the-box court form ([Justia](https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/ca2/22-1345/22-1345-2025-09-09.html), likely). Lesson for the product: *generic explanation of what a notice is and what such notices ordinarily require* is legal information; *telling this user what to file, argue, or choose* is legal advice, and UPL is state law that varies.

**Safe phrasing pattern for ProxyHealth (legal).**
- Header on every legal/immigration explanation: "This is general information about this type of document, not legal advice about your case. Only a licensed attorney or a DOJ-accredited representative can give you legal advice."
- Action plan verbs: "This notice lists a date of ___ (shown below). Notices like this usually require a response by that date. Before that date, talk to an attorney or DOJ-accredited representative (find one here)." Avoid "you should file/appeal/apply," "you qualify," "you are eligible."
- Referral line: "Use only attorneys in good standing or representatives on the DOJ roster. Notarios and immigration consultants cannot give legal advice."
- Scam cues surfaced when relevant (USCIS, verified): official sites/emails end in .gov; USCIS "will never ask you to pay fees to a person on the phone or by email" and does not accept "Western Union, MoneyGram, PayPal, Venmo, or gift cards."

**Medical disclaimers.** NLM: "It is not the intention of NLM to provide specific medical advice… NLM urges you to consult with a qualified health professional for diagnosis and for answers to your personal medical questions" ([NLM web policies](https://www.nlm.nih.gov/web_policies.html), verified). Apple 1.4.1 and Google Play both require the "consult a clinician" reminder (verified). Suggested wording: "This explains what your document says. It is not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Ask your doctor, nurse, or pharmacist what it means for you." Emergency/triage line (verified official numbers): "If this is an emergency, call 911. For a mental-health or suicide crisis, call or text 988 ([988lifeline.org](https://988lifeline.org/)). For a possible poisoning, call Poison Help 1-800-222-1222 ([poisonhelp.org](https://www.poisonhelp.org/))." Trigger the emergency card on keywords (chest pain, overdose, suicidal, anaphylaxis, stroke signs) in any language, and make it the first thing shown—not an LLM paragraph.

## 4. Gemini API terms and Google's prohibited-use rules

Source: [Gemini API Additional Terms of Service](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/terms), effective Mar 23 2026 (verified).

- **Unpaid Services** (AI Studio, free API quota): "Google uses the content you submit to the Services and any generated responses to provide, improve, and develop Google products and services and machine learning technologies"; "human reviewers may read, annotate, and process your API input and output"; Google's own instruction: "Do not submit sensitive, confidential, or personal information." → **Free tier is incompatible with this product.**
- **Paid Services** (Cloud Billing enabled): "Google doesn't use your prompts… or responses to improve our products"; prompts/responses logged "for a limited period of time, solely for detecting and preventing violations of the Prohibited Use Policy." Optional developer logging retains 55 days by default, adjustable to 7/14/28/55 ([logs policy](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/logs-policy), verified) — keep it off for document content.
- **Age:** "You must be 18 years of age or older to use the APIs. You also will not use the Services as part of a website, application, or other service… that is directed towards or is likely to be accessed by individuals under the age of 18."
- **Health restriction:** "You may not use the Services in clinical practice, to provide medical advice, or in any manner that is overseen by or requires clearance or approval from a medical device regulatory agency."
- **Disclaimer:** "Don't rely on the Services for medical, mental health, legal, financial, or other professional advice. Any content regarding those topics is provided for informational purposes only, does not constitute medical diagnosis or treatment, and is not a substitute for advice from a qualified professional." → ProxyHealth's own UX language must mirror this "informational only" framing.
- No clause requires labeling outputs as AI-generated, but Google warns the Services "may sometimes provide inaccurate or offensive content."

**Generative AI Prohibited Use Policy** ([policies.google.com](https://policies.google.com/terms/generative-ai/use-policy), last modified Dec 17 2024, verified). Relevant items: making "automated decisions that have a material detrimental impact on individual rights without human supervision in high-risk domains — for example, in employment, healthcare, finance, legal, housing, insurance, or social welfare"; "Facilitating misleading claims of expertise or capability in sensitive areas — for example in health, finance, government services, or the law, in order to deceive"; "Misrepresenting the provenance of generated content by claiming it was created solely by a human." → The app must not render eligibility determinations (benefits, relief) or "you will/will not be deported" style conclusions; keep a human (the user, and ideally an accredited rep) in every consequential decision.

**Vertex AI / Google Cloud alternative.** Google Cloud Service Specific Terms (verified via [cloud.google.com/terms/service-terms](https://cloud.google.com/terms/service-terms)) carry the same healthcare restriction ("Customer will not… use the Generative AI Services for clinical purposes (for clarity, non-clinical research, scheduling, or other administrative tasks is not restricted), as a substitute for professional medical advice, or in any manner that… requires clearance or approval from any applicable regulatory authority"), the same under-18 restriction, and incorporate the Prohibited Use Policy. Google Cloud will sign a BAA and lists specific Gemini products as HIPAA-covered ([Google Cloud HIPAA page](https://cloud.google.com/security/compliance/hipaa), verified); ProxyHealth doesn't need a BAA (not a CE/BA), but the enterprise path offers stronger contractual data-use terms and zero-data-retention options, which is a trust asset worth weighing against cost.

## 5. Accessibility baseline

**WCAG 2.2 Level AA** ([W3C TR](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/); new criteria at [What's new in 2.2](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/new-in-22/); all verified):
- 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum): text ≥ 4.5:1 (large text 3:1). 1.4.11 Non-text Contrast: UI components/graphics ≥ 3:1.
- 1.4.4 Resize Text: "up to 200 percent without loss of content or functionality." 1.4.10 Reflow: no two-dimensional scrolling at 320 CSS px width. 1.4.12 Text Spacing: survive line-height 1.5×, paragraph 2×, letter 0.12×, word 0.16×.
- 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum): "at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels," with Spacing/Equivalent/Inline/User-agent/Essential exceptions ([Understanding 2.5.8](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/target-size-minimum.html)); 2.5.5 (AAA) is 44×44.
- 2.4.7 Focus Visible; 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum) — sticky headers/toasts must not fully hide the focused element.
- 3.1.1 Language of Page (A) and 3.1.2 Language of Parts (AA): "The human language of each passage or phrase… can be programmatically determined." → For side-by-side source/translation, each pane needs its own `lang` (web), `accessibilityLanguage` (iOS) or `LocaleSpan` (Android) so screen readers switch voices.
- 3.3.7 Redundant Entry (A): previously entered info is auto-populated or selectable — relevant to multi-step action plans. 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication (Minimum): no cognitive-function test (e.g., CAPTCHA puzzle) without alternative. 4.1.3 Status Messages: announce "scan complete / 3 deadlines found" to AT.
- WCAG 2.2 removed 4.1.1 Parsing.

**Section 508** (federal agencies/procurement): Revised standards (final rule Jan 18 2017, compliance Jan 18 2018) require electronic content and software to "conform to Level A and Level AA Success Criteria and Conformance Requirements in WCAG 2.0" (E205.4, E207.2; [Access Board](https://www.access-board.gov/ict/), verified). Only binding if a federal body procures/deploys the app; state/local government deployers are governed by the DOJ ADA Title II web rule (WCAG 2.1 AA; not re-verified in this pass). Target WCAG 2.2 AA and you satisfy both.

**iOS (Apple HIG, [Accessibility](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/accessibility) and [Typography](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/typography), verified from the page data).** Default control size 44×44 pt, minimum 28×28 pt; "Consider spacing between controls as important as size." "Ideally, give people the option to enlarge text by at least 200 percent" via Dynamic Type; "aim to display as much useful text at the largest accessibility font size as you do at the largest standard font size"; avoid truncation; system text styles get Dynamic Type and AX1–AX5 sizes automatically, custom fonts must implement the same behavior.

**Android.** Touch targets "at least 48x48dp, separated by 8dp of space or more" (~9 mm) ([Android Accessibility Help](https://support.google.com/accessibility/android/answer/7101858), verified). Android 14+ font scaling "up to 200%" with a nonlinear curve; use `sp` for text *and* `lineHeight`, don't use `sp` for padding, `scaledDensity` is "no longer accurate," and "perform UI testing with the maximum font size enabled (200%)" ([Android 14 features](https://developer.android.com/about/versions/14/features), verified).

**RTL / bidi (Arabic, Persian/Dari, Pashto, Urdu, Hebrew).**
- Apple HIG [Right to left](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/right-to-left) (verified from page data): "Align a paragraph based on its language, not on the current context"; "Don't reverse the order of numerals in a specific number… a phone number, or a credit card number"; different RTL languages use different numerals ("Hebrew text uses Western Arabic numerals, whereas Arabic text might use either Western or Eastern Arabic numerals"); don't flip icons of real-world objects like clocks.
- Material Design [Bidirectionality](https://m1.material.io/usability/bidirectionality.html) (verified; M3 page at [m3.material.io](https://m3.material.io/foundations/layout/bidirectionality-rtl)): mirror layout, navigation order, directional arrows, progress bars; do **not** mirror numbers, untranslated text, clocks, media playback controls, non-directional icons; "Numbers, including icons containing numbers, must be localized for languages that use different numerals."
- W3C [Inline bidi markup](https://www.w3.org/International/articles/inline-bidi-markup/) (verified): wrap each opposite-direction phrase (case numbers, dates, English agency names, URLs, phone numbers) in an element with `dir`, or `<bdi>`/`dir="auto"` when direction is unknown; isolation beats embedding; use FSI/LRI/PDI controls only where markup is impossible (e.g., notification strings). This matters most for the extracted-deadline cards, where an English date/A-number sits inside Arabic or Urdu text.
- Urdu is conventionally set in Nastaliq: use Noto Nastaliq Urdu ([Google Fonts](https://fonts.google.com/noto/specimen/Noto+Nastaliq+Urdu)) and budget roughly 1.8–2.4× line-height so nuqtas/descenders don't clip ([google/fonts issue #7810](https://github.com/google/fonts/issues/7810), likely). Pashto and Dari use the Arabic script with extra letters; ensure fonts cover them (Noto Naskh Arabic does). Hebrew is RTL with LTR digits.

## 6. Languages US immigrant communities need — and where LLM quality is weak

**Census/ACS (verified).** 67.8 million (about 1 in 5) spoke a language other than English at home in 2019, triple 1980; top five: Spanish (62% of LOTE speakers), Chinese, Vietnamese, Tagalog, Arabic; share speaking English "less than very well": Vietnamese 57%, Chinese 52%, Spanish 39%, Arabic 35%, Tagalog 30% ([Census America Counts, Dec 2022](https://www.census.gov/library/stories/2022/12/languages-we-speak-in-united-states.html)). The 2017–2021 detailed tables cover "over 500 individual languages"; frequently cited next tier: French, Korean, Russian, Portuguese, Haitian Creole, Hindi, German ([Census release, Jun 3 2025](https://www.census.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2025/2017-2021-acs-language-use-tables.html); counts by language are in table [B16001](https://data.census.gov/table/ACSDT1Y2023.B16001), not pulled here). About 27.6 million people (8.7% of those 5+) are LEP ([USCCR fact sheet](https://www.usccr.gov/files/2026-05/lep-fact-sheet.pdf), verified).

**Recent humanitarian arrivals (verified/likely) → language mapping.**
- FY2024 refugee admissions 100,060: DRC 19,830; Afghanistan 14,680; Venezuela 11,350; Syria 11,240; Burma 7,330; Guatemala 5,030; Somalia 4,790; Nicaragua 2,950; Colombia 2,520; Eritrea 2,400 ([DHS OHSS FY24 Refugees Flow Report](https://ohss.dhs.gov/topics/immigration/refugees/annual-flow-report/fy-24-refugees-flow-report)). Refugee admissions were suspended in Jan 2025, so this cohort is the *installed base* now navigating benefits, housing and schools.
- DRC → Kinyarwanda ("the majority of Congolese refugees… speak Kinyarwanda"), Swahili, French, Lingala ([MN Dept of Health Congolese profile](https://www.health.state.mn.us/communities/rih/coe/profiles/congolese.html), likely). Afghanistan → Dari, Pashto (≈76,000 Operation Allies Welcome evacuees plus later SIV/refugee arrivals; [DHS OAW report](https://www.dhs.gov/sites/default/files/2022-03/DMO-OSEM%20-%20Department%20of%20Homeland%20Security%20Operation%20Allies%20Welcome%20Afghan%20Evacuee%20Report.pdf), likely). Burma → Burmese, Karen (S'gaw/Pwo), Chin dialects, Karenni, Kachin, Rohingya ([CDC refugee health profiles](https://www.cdc.gov/immigrantrefugeehealth/profiles/index.html), likely). Syria → Arabic. Eritrea → Tigrinya. Somalia → Somali. Guatemala → Spanish **and** Mam, K'iche', Q'anjob'al (among the 25 most common immigration-court languages; chronic interpreter shortages, [LA Public Press 2026](https://lapublicpress.org/2026/08/immigration-courts-indigenous-speakers-migrants-deportation-interpreters/), likely).
- Parole cohorts: ~532,000 CHNV parolees (110,240 Cubans, 211,040 Haitians, 93,080 Nicaraguans, 117,320 Venezuelans) → Spanish, Haitian Creole ([American Immigration Council](https://www.americanimmigrationcouncil.org/fact-sheet/biden-administrations-humanitarian-parole-program-cubans-haitians-nicaraguans-and/), likely); ~240,000 Uniting for Ukraine parolees → Ukrainian, Russian ([DHS U4U assessment](https://www.dhs.gov/sites/default/files/2024-12/2024_1104_dmo_plcy_uniting_for_ukraine_process_overview_and_assessment.pdf), likely). These groups face parole/TPS terminations and are heavy consumers of legal notices.
- Immigration court (FY2025 through Feb): Spanish 308,401 completed cases (34% represented), Portuguese 9,791, Mandarin 3,630, Russian 3,603, Punjabi 3,015, Arabic 2,374, Turkish 1,864, French 1,313; Creole speakers had the lowest representation at 21% ([TRAC report 757](https://tracreports.org/reports/757/), verified). Low representation = high reliance on tools like this one.

**Suggested tiering.** Tier 1 (full QA, human-reviewed glossaries): Spanish, Simplified & Traditional Chinese (note Cantonese speakers read Traditional), Vietnamese, Tagalog, Arabic, Haitian Creole, Portuguese (Brazilian), Russian, Ukrainian, Korean, French. Tier 2 (LLM + community review + prominent caveat): Dari, Pashto, Farsi, Urdu, Hindi, Punjabi, Bengali, Somali, Swahili, Amharic, Burmese, Nepali, Kinyarwanda. Tier 3 (experimental; always show source; encourage audio and human interpreter): Tigrinya, S'gaw Karen, Rohingya, Chin dialects, Mam/K'iche'/Q'anjob'al.

**Why the caveats.** LLM comprehension drops sharply outside high-resource languages—on Belebele, English ≈0.85–0.90 vs. some low-resource languages <0.32 ([multilingual functional evaluation, 2025](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2506.20793), likely). English–Tigrinya zero-shot MT scored chrF ≈10 ([arXiv 2509.20209](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2509.20209), likely). Even the FLORES-200 benchmark used to claim coverage has adequacy/fluency problems for some languages ([Languages Still Left Behind, 2025](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2508.20511); NLLB in [Nature 2024](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-024-07335-x), likely). Script realities: Rohingya has been a largely oral language; the Hanifi script is in Unicode but literacy in it is recent and uneven, and many Rohingya read Burmese, Urdu or Arabic script instead ([r12a Hanifi Rohingya notes](https://r12a.github.io/scripts/rohg/rhg.html), likely) → offer audio (TTS or recorded) as the primary modality. S'gaw Karen uses a Myanmar-based script needing Padauk/Noto Sans Myanmar and Unicode (not Zawgyi) rendering ([ScriptSource](https://www.scriptsource.org/cms/scripts/page.php?item_id=language_detail_font&key=ksw), likely). Tigrinya/Amharic use Ethiopic (Noto Sans Ethiopic).

**Design consequences.** Always show the source snippet beside the explanation (the user or a bilingual helper can check); label machine translations as such; add a per-message "Was this clear? / ¿Quedó claro?" thumbs plus free-text/voice feedback (also satisfies Play's flag requirement and NIST GV-3.2-004 below); route feedback on Tier 2–3 languages to community reviewers; keep numbers, dates, names and form numbers untranslated and bidi-isolated; provide a "call an interpreter" path (211, legal-aid lines) for Tier 3.

---

## 7. Safety patterns for LLM outputs (hallucinated deadlines, amounts, contacts)

**Why it is the top risk.** NIST AI 600-1 defines confabulation as GAI systems that "generate and confidently present erroneous or false content," warns that outputs "may also include confabulated logic or citations that purport to justify… the system's answer," and flags monitoring "when integrating GAI into applications involving consequential decision making" ([NIST AI 600-1](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/ai/NIST.AI.600-1.pdf), verified). Stanford RegLab found legal hallucination rates of 58–88% on verifiable questions about federal cases and that models "often fail to correct a user's incorrect legal assumptions" ([Stanford Law blog](https://law.stanford.edu/2024/01/11/hallucinating-law-legal-mistakes-with-large-language-models-are-pervasive/); [J. Legal Analysis 2024](https://academic.oup.com/jla/article/16/1/64/7699227), verified/likely); even RAG-based commercial legal tools still hallucinated at meaningful rates ([Hallucination-Free?, 2024](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2405.20362), likely). OWASP LLM09:2025 Misinformation prescribes RAG grounding, cross-verification and "human oversight and fact-checking processes, especially for critical or sensitive information" ([OWASP](https://genai.owasp.org/llmrisk/llm092025-misinformation/), verified).

**The stakes are asymmetric.** A respondent who misses a hearing "may result in the respondent being ordered removed 'in absentia'" and "There is no appeal from a removal order issued in absentia" ([EOIR Policy Manual 3.16](https://www.justice.gov/eoir/policy-manual-eoir/part-II/icpm/chapter-3-16), verified); a rescission motion for exceptional circumstances "must be filed within 180 days" ([EOIR 4.9](https://www.justice.gov/eoir/policy-manual-eoir/part-II/icpm/chapter-4-9), verified). BIA appeals "must be filed no later than 30 calendar days," counted by receipt, and "the Board does not have the authority to extend" ([BIA Practice Manual 3.5](https://www.justice.gov/eoir/policy-manual-eoir/part-III/bia/chapter-3-5), verified). Asylum "within 1 year of the date of your last arrival" ([USCIS](https://www.uscis.gov/humanitarian/refugees-and-asylum/asylum/obtaining-asylum-in-the-united-states), verified). Address changes: EOIR-33 within 5 business days of moving ([EOIR](https://www.justice.gov/eoir/update-respondent-or-alien-information), likely) vs. USCIS within 10 days ([USCIS](https://www.uscis.gov/addresschange), likely) — two different rules that a model will happily blur. Housing (eviction response windows) and benefits (recertification, fair-hearing windows) are state/program-specific.

**Mitigation architecture (recommendations).**
1. **Extraction is quotation, not generation.** Every extracted date, amount, case/receipt number, address, phone or URL must be returned with the verbatim source span and page/bounding box; a deterministic post-check rejects any value not found as an exact (or OCR-normalized) substring of the OCR text. Show the crop of the snippet next to the value ("Found on page 2: 'You must appear on 11/03/2026 at 8:30 AM'").
2. **No derived dates without the rule.** If a deadline is computed (e.g., "30 days from the date of this decision"), show the formula, the anchor date from the document, and the cited rule, and label it "estimate — confirm with the sender or your representative." Never let the model do date arithmetic silently; do it in code and display both inputs.
3. **Confidence flags** driven by OCR confidence, digit ambiguity (1/7, 0/8, 3/8), handwriting, partial pages, and model self-consistency (ask twice, compare). Low confidence → amber card + "Re-scan this part" CTA.
4. **"Verify with the sender" CTA on every deadline/amount**, with the sender's contact taken *from the document or the vetted DB only*.
5. **Contacts come only from the vetted DB.** The model is never allowed to emit a phone number, URL, address or organization name; the UI resolves entities to the curated directory (EOIR rosters, EOIR pro bono list, state bars, 211, 988, Poison Help, official .gov pages). Enforce with a regex/entity filter on model output that strips or blocks any digits-that-look-like-phone or URLs not present in the source document. USCIS scam guidance (.gov only; no gift-card payments) should be surfaced when a document requests payment.
6. **Human in the loop for consequences.** Per Google's Prohibited Use Policy, no automated eligibility or outcome determinations; the action plan ends in a referral, not a decision.
7. **Feedback and monitoring.** In-app flag on every output (Play requirement); NIST suggested actions GV-3.2-004 ("Establish policies for user feedback mechanisms for GAI systems which include thorough instructions and any mechanisms for recourse"), GV-5.1-002 ("Document interactions with GAI systems to users prior to interactive activities, particularly in contexts involving more significant risks"), MS-2.5-003 ("Review and verify sources and citations in GAI system outputs during pre-deployment risk measurement and ongoing monitoring"), MG-3.2-004 ("Evaluate user reported problematic content and integrate feedback into system updates") (all verified from the NIST text). Build a gold set of real (redacted) notices per document type and language and measure extraction precision/recall and hallucinated-entity rate before each model/prompt change.
8. **Prompt-injection and adversarial documents.** Treat document text as untrusted data: system prompt must instruct the model to ignore instructions embedded in the image; scam letters *are* adversarial content.
9. **Scope guardrails in the prompt.** The model explains, extracts, and lists generic next steps; it refuses to interpret lab values clinically, to predict case outcomes, to determine eligibility, or to draft documents purporting to be from an agency.
10. **Transparency copy.** Each explanation footer: "Generated by AI from your document. It can be wrong. Check the highlighted text and confirm dates with the sender or a professional."

warnings: Do NOT ship on the Gemini free/unpaid tier. Google uses unpaid-tier prompts and outputs to improve its products with human review and tells developers not to submit personal information; sending medical or immigration documents there would contradict any 'we don't store your data' promise, likely count as third-party sharing on both stores' privacy forms, and could be an 'unauthorized disclosure' breach under the FTC Health Breach Notification Rule. Use a billing-enabled (paid) project or Google Cloud/Vertex enterprise terms, and keep optional developer logging off for document content.

The Gemini API terms prohibit apps 'directed towards or likely to be accessed by individuals under 18' and require 18+ users. Rate the app 18+ in both stores, do not market it to students, and frame school-document features for parents/guardians.

Gemini/Google Cloud terms forbid use 'to provide medical advice' or 'as a substitute for professional medical advice,' and Google's Prohibited Use Policy forbids automated decisions with material detrimental impact in healthcare, legal, housing or social-welfare domains without human supervision. Prompts and UX must keep outputs at 'what this document says' plus referral; never output eligibility, prognosis, case-outcome, or 'you should file X' conclusions.

Apple 5.1.2(i) (since Nov 13 2025) requires an in-app disclosure and explicit permission BEFORE personal data is shared with third-party AI. A privacy-policy link alone will be rejected. Show a consent screen naming Google Gemini before the first scan, and record the consent.
Apple 5.1.1(ix): submit from an organization (legal entity) developer account, not an individual account, because the app operates in healthcare and handles sensitive information.

Apple 5.1.3(ii) bars storing personal health information in iCloud; exclude extracted medical data from iCloud backup/sync. Apple 5.1.2(vi) and 5.1.3(i) bar any analytics/marketing use of camera-derived or health data, including by SDKs; keep analytics SDKs away from document content entirely.

Google Play requires: the Health apps declaration form, a not-a-medical-device statement plus a 'consult a healthcare professional' reminder, prominent in-app disclosure and affirmative consent before collecting sensitive data, an in-app report/flag control on AI outputs, no READ_MEDIA_IMAGES/VIDEO permission (use camera + system photo picker), and, if accounts exist, deletion in-app AND via a web page.

Answer Apple's privacy label and Google's Data safety form consistently and truthfully. 'Data Not Collected' for document content is defensible only if inference is transient, nothing is retained server-side, Gemini is on paid/service-provider terms, and no SDK sees the content. Any account, cloud sync, or crash-reporting that includes document text changes the answers.

HIPAA does not apply to a consumer-chosen app, but the FTC Health Breach Notification Rule very likely does (apps that track diagnoses, medications, treatment are 'health care services or supplies'; camera + user input + calendar plausibly meet 'multiple sources'). Plan for 60-day breach notice, treat unauthorized sharing as a breach, and obtain counsel's written opinion. If any clinic, plan, school district or legal-aid grantee contracts you to deploy the app for its clients, re-analyze business-associate status.

State law adds obligations: Washington's My Health My Data Act (consent to collect/share consumer health data; private right of action) and California's CPRA (immigration status and health are 'sensitive personal information'; offer limit-use rights). Immigration status is inferable from nearly every document the app processes.

Legal outputs must stay on the 'legal information' side of the UPL line, which is state law and was just enforced in Upsolve v. James (2d Cir. 2025). Explain document types and generic next steps; do not apply the law to the user's facts, recommend a filing, or predict outcomes. Every legal/immigration screen carries 'not legal advice; only a licensed attorney or DOJ-accredited representative can advise you,' and referrals go only to the EOIR rosters, EOIR pro bono list, or state-bar-verified attorneys.

Never let the model draft or complete official forms/letters or produce anything that could pass as agency documentation (Google Play treats AI-generated official documentation enabling dishonesty as prohibited; it also invites notario-style misuse).

Medical outputs: describe, don't interpret. Explaining a lab value's meaning for the user edges toward FDA-regulated 'interpret or analyze' functions and toward Gemini's 'medical advice' restriction. Always show the clinician reminder and an emergency card (911 / 988 call-or-text / Poison Help 1-800-222-1222) triggered by emergency keywords in every language, rendered from fixed copy, not from the LLM.

Hallucinated dates, amounts, and contacts are the highest-severity failure. Enforce in code: every extracted value must match a verbatim span in the OCR text (show the crop); derived deadlines display the anchor date, the rule and its source and are labeled estimates; the model is never permitted to emit phone numbers, URLs, addresses or organization names — resolve all contacts from the vetted directory and strip anything else; add confidence flags for OCR ambiguity (1/7, 0/8, handwriting, partial pages) and a 'verify with the sender' CTA on every deadline.

Deadlines are agency- and jurisdiction-specific and unforgiving (in absentia removal with no appeal; 30-day BIA appeal by receipt; 180-day rescission window; 1-year asylum bar; EOIR-33 within 5 business days vs. AR-11 within 10 days; state-specific eviction and benefits windows). Do not let the model 'know' deadlines from memory; only surface what the document states or what a maintained rules table cites.

Treat document images as untrusted input. Scam letters and phishing notices are adversarial content; instruct the model to ignore embedded instructions, and surface USCIS scam cues (.gov only; no gift-card/wire/Venmo payments; 'guaranteed results' red flags) when a document requests payment or personal data.

Translation quality collapses for low-resource languages (Tigrinya, Karen, Rohingya, Mayan languages, many African languages). Always show the source text side by side, label machine translation, keep numbers/dates/form numbers untranslated and bidi-isolated, offer audio for oral-literacy communities (Rohingya), collect 'Was this clear?' feedback per message, and route those languages to human review or interpreter referral rather than promising coverage.

Accessibility is not optional for this population: meet WCAG 2.2 AA (24×24 CSS px targets minimum; aim for 44 pt iOS / 48 dp Android), 4.5:1 contrast, 200% text scaling without truncation (test iOS AX5 and Android 200% nonlinear scaling), visible/unobscured focus, and per-pane language tagging so screen readers switch voices between source and translation. Urdu Nastaliq needs ~1.8–2.4× line height; Arabic-script locales differ on Eastern vs Western digits; never reverse digit order in numbers.

Minimize what exists to be subpoenaed or purchased: no server persistence of images or extracted fields by default, on-device redaction of A-numbers/SSNs/receipt numbers before inference, device-level encryption at rest, no cloud backup of extracted data, no ad/analytics SDKs, and a one-tap local wipe. ICE has bought commercial app-derived data; design as if any server-side store will eventually be requested.

Keep claims modest and verifiable in store listings, onboarding and marketing. FTC Act §5 and both stores' rules punish privacy or accuracy promises that the implementation does not literally keep, and Apple 2.3.1 requires new features to be described specifically in Notes for Review.
